title: Choose Building Blocks by Their Guarantees
summary: Connect core concepts, technologies and reusable patterns without turning an interview into a shopping list.
body:
Learn three layers together: a concept explains a constraint, a technology supplies a mechanism, and a pattern combines mechanisms to solve a recurring problem. Knowing a product name without its guarantees is not enough to defend a design.

## Start from a request

Consider accepting an order and later sending a receipt. The order needs a durable record. Email delivery is slower and may fail independently. This gives you a reason for a transactional database and an asynchronous worker; it does not automatically require sharding or a globally replicated log.

## Match a component to its job

| Building block | A reason to use it | A question you must answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relational database | Transactions, constraints and flexible queries | What must commit atomically? Which indexes support reads? |
| Key-value or document store | Access patterns that map naturally to keys or documents | What consistency, transaction and query guarantees are actually available? |
| Cache | Avoid repeated expensive reads | What is the source of truth, and how stale may a response be? |
| Queue or event log | Decouple producers from processing | Can messages repeat or arrive out of order? How do consumers recover? |
| Object storage | Store large files separately from metadata | How are access, upload completion and retention controlled? |
| Search index | Support text search or specialized retrieval | How does the index catch up with the authoritative data? |
| Load balancer | Route requests across healthy instances | What happens to sessions and in-flight work when an instance fails? |

These categories are not absolute limitations. Some document stores support transactions and some relational databases scale horizontally. Choose a specific system only after checking the workload and the guarantees you need.

## Compose mechanisms into patterns

A cache-aside read asks the cache first, falls back to the database and fills the cache. An asynchronous processing path stores work durably before workers act. An idempotent consumer recognizes repeated delivery before applying an effect. Each pattern introduces its own state and failure cases.

For the receipt example, putting the order in a database and publishing a message are two writes that can fail separately. A transactional outbox can record the order and an event in one database transaction; a dispatcher forwards the event later. Forwarding may repeat, so the consumer still needs duplicate handling. Naming an outbox is not a substitute for explaining this flow.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|"POST /orders"| API["Order API"]
    API -->|"one transaction"| DB[("orders + outbox rows")]
    DB --> RL["Outbox relay"]
    RL --> Q[["Order events"]]
    Q --> W["Receipt worker"]
    W -->|"skip if seen"| SEEN[("Processed event IDs")]
    W --> EM["Email provider"]
```

The order and its event commit together, so there is never an order without an event or an event without an order. The relay publishes outbox rows and marks them sent; if it crashes between publishing and marking, it publishes again, which is why the worker records processed event IDs before sending a receipt.

## Scale only when a bottleneck justifies it

First identify whether pressure comes from reads, writes, data size, a hot key or an external dependency. An extra read replica cannot fix a write bottleneck. A cache cannot guarantee correctness for an invariant enforced only in stale data. More queue workers can overload a downstream provider unless concurrency is bounded.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["Measured bottleneck"] --> R["Repeated reads"]
    P --> WR["Write volume or data size"]
    P --> BL["Large files"]
    P --> SR["Text or geo search"]
    P --> HK["One hot key"]
    P --> SD["Slow dependency"]
    R --> R2["Cache or read replicas"]
    WR --> W2["Batching or partitioning"]
    BL --> B2["Object storage and CDN"]
    SR --> S2["Search index fed by change events"]
    HK --> H2["Split key, cache, or limit"]
    SD --> D2["Queue with bounded workers"]
```

Each pressure maps to a different mechanism, and none of them fixes the others: replicas do nothing for write volume, and partitioning does nothing for one hot key. Name the pressure first, then pick the block, then state the new failure mode the block introduces (cache staleness, replica lag, index lag, queue backlog).

## Try it

Design the first version of a file-sharing service. Pick a home for file bytes, metadata and access permissions. Explain one upload and one download. Add a search index only if search is a requirement, and explain what a user sees before the index catches up.

## Continue learning

Work through Foundations for vocabulary, Data & Storage for persistence guarantees, and the reliability and distributed modules for failure-handling patterns. Then practise a full case study before reading its reference discussion.

## Further reading

- [microservices.io: Transactional outbox](https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html) describes the outbox pattern and its relay options.
- [Designing Data-Intensive Applications](https://dataintensive.net/) explains the guarantees behind databases, logs and derived data systems.
keyTakeaways: Choose mechanisms to satisfy requirements, not to maximize the number of technologies in a diagram.
Explain transactions, consistency, delivery and recovery guarantees explicitly.
A database plus a queue creates a dual-write problem; an outbox still requires duplicate handling.
Identify the bottleneck before selecting a scaling technique.
